title: Why Mahlon and Chilion Died Before Ruth’s Story Truly Began
paragraphs: Why Mahlon and Chilion Died Before Ruth’s Story Truly Began
There are some graves in Scripture that almost nobody stops to visit.
Not physically. Emotionally. Spiritually.
We preach David. We quote Paul. We cry with Joseph. We stand amazed at Ruth.
But almost nobody talks about the two silent graves standing at the entrance of Ruth’s story.
Mahlon. Chilion.
Two brothers. Two husbands. Two funerals.
And if they had lived… Ruth’s story may never have unfolded the way heaven intended.
That is the terrifying mystery hidden inside the Book of Ruth.
Sometimes the beginning of redemption is buried beneath a tragedy nobody understands.
The Book of Ruth does not begin with romance. It begins with famine. Loss. Migration. Disappointment. Death.
The opening chapter feels less like a love story and more like God has abandoned an entire family.
But hidden inside the darkness is one of the deepest revelations in Scripture: God can use even devastating loss to position somebody for covenant redemption.
And many people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Because there are seasons where your entire life feels like Chapter One of Ruth.
Everything keeps dying before the promise ever begins.
Dreams die. Relationships die. Hope dies. Faith weakens. Prayers feel unanswered.
You keep asking God why things collapsed before they even had the chance to live.
That is exactly where Naomi was.
The Hebrew text introduces the story this way:
"וַיְהִי בִּימֵי שְׁפֹט הַשֹּׁפְטִים" (Vayehi bimei shefot hashoftim)
Translated literally: “And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged.”
This is not random historical detail. It is spiritual atmosphere.
The era of the Judges was one of the darkest periods in Israel’s history.
Judges 21:25 says:
"בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה"
“In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes.”
Moral confusion. Spiritual compromise. National instability.
And then came famine.
The Hebrew word used in Ruth 1:1 is:
"רָעָב" (ra’av)
Not just hunger. Desolation. Scarcity. Emptiness.
Bethlehem — the “House of Bread” — had no bread.
Even the place associated with provision became barren.
And isn’t that how suffering feels sometimes?
The very places you expected life from suddenly become empty.
The marriage dries up. The church wounds you. The people you trusted disappear. The dream collapses.
Naomi’s husband Elimelech decides to leave Bethlehem and journey into Moab.
Moab was not spiritually neutral territory.
Moab carried a painful history with Israel. The Moabites descended from Lot through an incestuous union recorded in Genesis 19. They later opposed Israel repeatedly.
Yet desperation can make people settle in places they once would have avoided.
And people still do this today.
When fear grows louder than faith, compromise begins looking practical.
The Hebrew name “Elimelech” means:
"אֱלִי מֶלֶךְ" (Eli Melech)
“My God is King.”
But ironically, the man whose name proclaimed God’s kingship fled the covenant land during crisis.
Then Scripture quietly introduces his sons:
Mahlon. Chilion.
Their names themselves are haunting.
Many Hebrew scholars connect Mahlon (מַחְלוֹן) with sickness or weakness. Chilion (כִּלְיוֹן) is often connected to frailty, wasting away, or destruction.
Imagine carrying names that sound like prophecy over suffering.
And after entering Moab, tragedy begins falling like dominoes.
Elimelech dies.
Then the sons marry Moabite women: Orpah and Ruth.
Then after about ten years… both sons die too.
Three graves. One widow. Two shattered daughters-in-law.
The Hebrew text says:
"וַתִּשָּׁאֵר הָאִשָּׁה" (Vatisha’er ha’ishah)
“And the woman was left.”
Left.
That word carries the weight of abandonment. Survival. Aftermath.
Some people reading this know what it means to feel “left.”
Left behind after divorce. Left grieving after funerals. Left wondering why God allowed the collapse. Left carrying trauma nobody else sees.
Naomi did not merely lose family members. She lost her future.
In ancient Israelite culture, sons represented legacy, protection, inheritance, continuity, survival.
And now both sons were dead.
Mahlon and Chilion died before the real story even began.
Why?
That question unsettles many believers because it touches the mystery of divine providence.
The text never explicitly says God killed them. Scripture is careful.
But the narrative forces readers to wrestle with something uncomfortable: sometimes God allows devastating endings because He sees a redemptive future hidden beyond them.

Without those deaths, Ruth likely remains in Moab. Without widowhood, Ruth may never cling to Naomi. Without emptiness, Bethlehem is never revisited. Without loss, Boaz never enters the story. Without Boaz, the lineage leading to David is altered.
And without that lineage… the earthly genealogy leading toward Jesus the Messiah is affected.
Matthew 1:5 specifically includes Ruth in the genealogy of Christ.
That means heaven was writing a redemption story through human heartbreak.
Not because suffering is good. But because God is powerful enough to redeem what suffering destroys.
That distinction matters.
God is not cruel. He is sovereign.
And sovereignty often looks confusing while we are standing inside the storm.
Naomi certainly did not feel blessed.
When she returns to Bethlehem, she says:
“Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara.”
In Hebrew:
"אַל־תִּקְרֶאנָה לִי נָעֳמִי קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא" (Al tikrenah li Naomi, krena li Mara)
Naomi means “pleasant.” Mara means “bitter.”
There are people reading this who know exactly what bitterness born from disappointment feels like.
You used to feel alive. Now you feel numb.
You used to trust easily. Now your heart protects itself.
You used to pray with confidence. Now you pray exhausted.
Naomi says:
"כִּי־הֵמַר שַׁדַּי לִי מְאֹד"
“For the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.”
This is raw honesty. Not polished religion.
One reason Ruth remains so emotionally powerful is because Scripture does not sanitize grief.
The Bible never pretends faithful people do not suffer.
And that is important because modern culture often sells a distorted version of faith where obedience supposedly guarantees comfort.
But Ruth destroys that illusion.
Faithful people still bury loved ones. Faithful people still cry at night. Faithful people still question God. Faithful people still walk through seasons where heaven feels silent.
Yet somehow… God still moves.
And then the story changes.
Not suddenly. Quietly.
Ruth makes one of the most powerful covenant declarations in all Scripture.
"כִּי אֶל־אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ" (Ki el-asher telchi elech)
“For wherever you go, I will go.”
"עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי"
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
This is more than emotional loyalty. This is covenant surrender.
Ruth was a Moabite. An outsider. A foreigner. Someone many Israelites would have viewed with suspicion.
Yet God was already preparing to use the rejected woman in the lineage of the Messiah.
That alone preaches.
Because some of the people God uses most powerfully are the people society overlooks.
The broken. The ashamed. The outsider. The one with a painful history. The one who thinks their story ended in Moab.
And perhaps that is one hidden reason Mahlon and Chilion died before Ruth’s story truly began.
Their deaths exposed Ruth’s heart.
Would she stay in Moab? Or would she pursue the God of Israel despite uncertainty?
Sometimes suffering reveals whether love was conditional.
And Ruth stayed.
Not because she understood everything. But because covenant love held her.
That is one of the deepest pictures of discipleship in the Old Testament.
Real faith does not stay only when life feels rewarding. Real faith clings even while grieving.
Many believers love God when prayers are answered. But Ruth loved through loss.
That is rare.
And heaven noticed.
Then comes Boaz.
Not accidentally. Providentially.
The Hebrew concept operating throughout Ruth is often connected to divine providence hidden beneath ordinary events.
Ruth “happens” to glean in Boaz’s field. Boaz “happens” to notice her. Naomi “happens” to have a kinsman redeemer.
But faithful readers recognize something deeper.
God was arranging redemption while the characters still thought they were surviving tragedy.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to hear that.
Just because your life feels shattered does not mean God stopped writing.
Some chapters only make sense when viewed from the ending.
The Hebrew term for “kinsman redeemer” is:
"גֹּאֵל" (go’el)
A redeemer. One who restores. One who rescues family inheritance. One who intervenes on behalf of the vulnerable.
Boaz becomes a prophetic shadow pointing toward Jesus Christ.
Because humanity also stood spiritually widowed, bankrupt, vulnerable, and unable to redeem itself.
Then Christ stepped into the story.
The Greek New Testament describes redemption with words like:
"ἀπολύτρωσις" (apolýtrōsis)
Meaning: release through ransom, deliverance, redemption secured by payment.
Jesus became the greater Redeemer.
Where Boaz redeemed Ruth’s future, Christ redeems eternal souls.
Where Boaz restored inheritance, Christ restores relationship with God.
Where Boaz covered Ruth, Christ covers sinners with grace.
And suddenly the deaths of Mahlon and Chilion become part of a far bigger story.
Not random. Not meaningless.
Painful. Yes. But not purposeless.
There are people reading this right now still angry at God because something ended.
You thought the relationship would survive. You thought the ministry would flourish. You thought the diagnosis would disappear. You thought the prayer would be answered differently.
And because something died, you assumed your story died too.
But Ruth proves something astonishing: sometimes God allows one chapter to close because another covenant chapter is waiting beyond the burial.
Naomi thought she returned empty. But she returned carrying Ruth.
And Ruth was carrying destiny.
Eventually Ruth and Boaz have a son named Obed. Obed fathers Jesse. Jesse fathers David.
And generations later… Jesus Christ enters human history through that lineage.
The women weeping in Ruth 4:14 tell Naomi:
“Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer.”
Notice the reversal.
The woman who once said, “I am empty,” now holds redemption in her arms.
This is why believers must be careful not to judge their story too early.
Friday looked hopeless before Sunday arrived.
The cross looked like defeat before resurrection revealed victory.
And your current pain may not be the final chapter either.
Mahlon and Chilion died before Ruth’s story truly began because sometimes God permits endings that human beings cannot yet understand.
But the God of Scripture specializes in bringing resurrection out of ruins.
That does not erase grief. It redeems it.
And maybe that is where this article becomes personal.
Because many people scrolling tonight are secretly carrying funerals in their soul.
Not physical funerals alone.
The funeral of innocence. The funeral of trust. The funeral of old dreams. The funeral of relationships. The funeral of the person you used to be.
And somewhere deep inside, you keep asking:
“Why did this die before my story even began?”
Ruth answers softly:
Because God still writes beautiful things after graves.
And if somebody you love is grieving, discouraged, spiritually exhausted, or questioning God because of painful endings, share this with them.
Some people are one moment away from giving up completely. They need to know God still writes redemption stories after loss.
Some endings are not proof God abandoned you. Sometimes they are the doorway where redemption quietly begins.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Namatay Sina Mahlon at Chilion Bago Tunay na Nagsimula ang Kuwento ni Ruth
May mga libingan sa Bibliya na halos walang tumitigil para alalahanin.
Hindi pisikal. Kundi emosyonal. Espirituwal.
Pinapangaral natin si David. Iniisip natin si Jose. Hinahangaan natin si Pablo. Naiiyak tayo kay Ruth.
Pero bihirang pag-usapan ng mga tao ang dalawang tahimik na libingan sa simula ng aklat ni Ruth.
Mahlon. Chilion.
Dalawang magkapatid. Dalawang asawa. Dalawang maagang kamatayan.
At kung nabuhay sana sila… maaaring hindi kailanman nangyari ang kuwento ni Ruth sa paraan na itinakda ng langit.
Iyan ang mabigat na hiwagang nakatago sa Aklat ni Ruth.
Minsan, ang simula ng pagtubos ay nakabaon muna sa trahedyang hindi maintindihan ng tao.
Ang Aklat ni Ruth ay hindi nagsisimula sa pag-ibig. Nagsisimula ito sa taggutom. Pagkawala. Paglipat. Kalungkutan. Kamatayan.
Parang iniwan na ng Diyos ang isang buong pamilya.
Pero sa ilalim ng lahat ng dilim na iyon, may isang malalim na katotohanan: Kayang gamitin ng Diyos kahit ang pinakamasakit na pagkawala upang ihanda ang isang tao para sa pagtubos.
At maraming taong nagbabasa nito ang alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Dahil may mga panahon sa buhay na parang Chapter One ka ng Ruth.
Lahat namamatay bago pa magsimula ang pangako.
Namamatay ang pangarap. Namamatay ang relasyon. Humihina ang pananampalataya. Nawawala ang pag-asa.
Paulit-ulit mong tinatanong ang Diyos: “Bakit ito nawala bago pa man talaga nagsimula?”
Ganiyan si Naomi.
Ganito ipinakilala ng Hebrew text ang kuwento:
"וַיְהִי בִּימֵי שְׁפֹט הַשֹּׁפְטִים" (Vayehi bimei shefot hashoftim)
“At nangyari sa panahon na ang mga hukom ay namamahala…”
Hindi ito simpleng historical detail. Ito ay espirituwal na atmosphere.
Madilim ang panahon ng mga Hukom.
Sinasabi ng Judges 21:25:
"בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה"
“Sa mga araw na iyon ay walang hari sa Israel; bawat tao ay ginagawa kung ano ang tama sa sarili niyang paningin.”
Magulong moralidad. Kompromisong espirituwal. Kalituhan.
At pagkatapos… dumating ang taggutom.
Ang salitang ginamit sa Hebrew ay:
"רָעָב" (ra’av)
Hindi lang simpleng gutom. Kundi kakulangan. Pagkawasak. Kawalan.
Ang Bethlehem — “Bahay ng Tinapay” — ay wala nang tinapay.
Maging ang lugar na dapat may kasaganaan ay naging tuyot.
At ganiyan din minsan ang sakit.
Ang mismong lugar na inaasahan mong magbibigay buhay… biglang nawawalan ng laman.
Ang relasyon nasisira. Ang tahanan nagiging malamig. Ang mga taong pinagkatiwalaan mo nawawala.
Dahil sa desperasyon, iniwan ni Elimelech ang Bethlehem at pumunta sa Moab kasama ang kaniyang pamilya.
Ang Moab ay hindi simpleng ibang lugar lang.
May mabigat itong kasaysayan laban sa Israel.
Pero kapag takot ang nangunguna sa puso, kahit ang maling lugar nagmumukhang tama.
At ganiyan pa rin hanggang ngayon.
Kapag mas malakas ang takot kaysa pananampalataya, nagsisimulang magmukhang praktikal ang kompromiso.
Ang pangalan ni Elimelech sa Hebrew ay:
"אֱלִי מֶלֶךְ" (Eli Melech)
“Ito ay nangangahulugang: Ang Diyos ko ay Hari.”
Pero ang lalaking may pangalang nagpapatotoo tungkol sa paghahari ng Diyos… umalis sa lupang pangako noong panahon ng krisis.
Pagkatapos ay ipinakilala ang kaniyang mga anak:
Mahlon. Chilion.
Nakakatindig-balahibo maging ang kahulugan ng kanilang mga pangalan.
Ang “Mahlon” ay konektado sa sakit o kahinaan. Ang “Chilion” naman ay konektado sa panghihina o pagkawasak.
Parang may anino ng paghihirap sa kanilang buhay.
Pagkatapos mamatay ni Elimelech, nag-asawa ang magkapatid ng mga babaeng Moabita: Orpah at Ruth.
At matapos ang halos sampung taon… namatay din sina Mahlon at Chilion.
Tatlong libingan. Isang biyuda. Dalawang babaeng wasak ang mundo.
Ganito sinasabi ng Hebrew text:
"וַתִּשָּׁאֵר הָאִשָּׁה" (Vatisha’er ha’ishah)
“At ang babae ay naiwan.”
Naiwan.
May bigat ang salitang iyon.
Naiwan pagkatapos ng sakit. Naiwan pagkatapos ng pagkawala. Naiwan habang nagpapatuloy ang mundo.
Maraming taong nagbabasa nito ang alam ang pakiramdam ng pagiging “naiwan.”
Naiwan matapos iwan. Naiwan matapos mawalan. Naiwan matapos mailibing ang isang mahal sa buhay. Naiwan habang pilit ngumiting sugatan.
Hindi lang pamilya ang nawala kay Naomi. Parang nawala rin ang kaniyang kinabukasan.
Sa kultura noon, ang mga anak na lalaki ay simbolo ng pangalan, proteksiyon, mana, at seguridad.
At ngayon… wala na silang lahat.
Namatay sina Mahlon at Chilion bago pa man tunay na nagsimula ang kuwento ni Ruth.
Pero bakit?
Iyan ang tanong na mahirap sagutin.
Hindi tahasang sinasabi ng Bibliya na pinatay sila ng Diyos. Maingat ang Kasulatan.
Pero malinaw na ipinapakita ng kuwento na minsan pinapayagan ng Diyos ang mga masakit na pagtatapos dahil may mas malaking pagtubos Siyang nakikita sa hinaharap.

Kung hindi namatay sina Mahlon at Chilion, maaaring hindi kailanman sumama si Ruth kay Naomi. Kung hindi naging biyuda si Ruth, maaaring hindi siya bumalik sa Bethlehem. Kung hindi siya bumalik sa Bethlehem, maaaring hindi niya nakilala si Boaz.
At kung walang Boaz… maaapektuhan ang linya ng lahi na hahantong kay David.
At mula sa linyang iyon… darating si Jesucristo.
Sinasabi ng Mateo 1:5 na kasama si Ruth sa genealogy ni Jesus.
Ibig sabihin, habang umiiyak ang tao sa lupa… nagsusulat ang langit ng kuwento ng pagtubos.
Hindi dahil mabuti ang pagdurusa. Kundi dahil kayang tubusin ng Diyos kahit ang winasak ng sakit.
Magkaiba iyon.
Hindi malupit ang Diyos. Soberano Siya.
At minsan, mahirap maintindihan ang soberanya ng Diyos habang nasa gitna ka pa ng unos.
Hindi naramdaman ni Naomi na pinagpala siya.
Pagbalik niya sa Bethlehem sinabi niya:
“Huwag ninyo akong tawaging Naomi. Tawagin ninyo akong Mara.”
Sa Hebrew:
"אַל־תִּקְרֶאנָה לִי נָעֳמִי קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא"
Ang Naomi ay nangangahulugang “kaaya-aya.” Ang Mara ay “mapait.”
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na parang ganiyan din ang puso.
Dati masaya. Ngayon manhid.
Dati nagtitiwala. Ngayon takot nang masaktan.
Dati malakas manalangin. Ngayon pagod na.
At iyan ang dahilan kung bakit napakatotoo ng Aklat ni Ruth.
Hindi nito tinatakpan ang sakit. Hindi nito pinaplastik ang pagdurusa.
Ang Bibliya ay hindi fairy tale.
Ipinapakita nitong kahit ang mga taong may pananampalataya ay umiiyak din.
Pero kahit ganoon… kumikilos pa rin ang Diyos.
At pagkatapos, nagbago ang kuwento.
Hindi biglaan. Tahimik.
Sinabi ni Ruth kay Naomi:
"כִּי אֶל־אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ"
“Kung saan ka pupunta, sasama ako.”
"עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהָיִךְ אֱלֹהָי"
“Ang iyong bayan ay magiging aking bayan, at ang iyong Diyos ay magiging aking Diyos.”
Hindi lang ito emosyon. Ito ay covenant. Pagsuko. Katapatan.
Si Ruth ay isang Moabita. Dayuhan. Outsider.
Pero ginagamit na pala siya ng Diyos para maging bahagi ng linya ng Mesiyas.
Napakalalim noon.
Dahil madalas ginagamit ng Diyos ang mga taong minamaliit ng lipunan.
Ang sugatan. Ang may nakaraan. Ang itinapon. Ang nagkamali. Ang akala nilang tapos na ang kuwento nila.
At baka isa sa mga dahilan kung bakit namatay sina Mahlon at Chilion ay upang mahayag kung sino talaga si Ruth.
Mananatili ba siya sa Moab? O hahabulin niya ang Diyos ng Israel kahit hindi malinaw ang hinaharap?
Minsan, ang sakit ang naglalantad kung tunay ang pag-ibig.
At nanatili si Ruth.
Hindi dahil naiintindihan niya ang lahat. Kundi dahil pinili niyang kumapit.
Iyan ang tunay na pananampalataya.
Hindi lang nananatili kapag maganda ang buhay. Nanatili kahit masakit.
Pagkatapos ay dumating si Boaz.
Hindi aksidente. Kundi providence.
Parang nagkataon lang ang lahat. Nagkataong sa bukid ni Boaz napunta si Ruth. Nagkataong napansin siya.
Pero ang totoo?
Habang iniisip nilang wasak ang buhay nila… tahimik nang inaayos ng Diyos ang pagtubos.
At baka may kailangang makarinig nito ngayon.
Dahil lang wasak ang kasalukuyang chapter mo, hindi ibig sabihin tapos na ang sinusulat ng Diyos.
May mga bahagi ng kuwento na naiintindihan lang kapag nakita mo na ang ending.
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “kinsman redeemer” ay:
"גֹּאֵל" (go’el)
Tagatubos. Tagapagligtas. Tagapagbalik.
Si Boaz ay larawan ni Cristo.
Dahil ang sangkatauhan rin ay nawalan. Nalugmok. Hindi kayang iligtas ang sarili.
At pagkatapos… pumasok si Jesus sa kuwento.
Sa Greek New Testament, ginagamit ang salitang:
"ἀπολύτρωσις" (apolýtrōsis)
Ibig sabihin: redemption, paglaya, pagtubos sa pamamagitan ng kabayaran.
Si Jesus ang dakilang Redeemer.
Kung paanong tinubos ni Boaz si Ruth, tinutubos ni Cristo ang makasalanang tao.
Kung paanong ibinalik ni Boaz ang pag-asa, ibinabalik ni Cristo ang relasyon natin sa Diyos.
At biglang nagkaroon ng mas malaking kahulugan ang pagkamatay nina Mahlon at Chilion.
Masakit. Oo.
Pero hindi walang saysay.
May mga taong galit pa rin sa Diyos dahil may namatay na chapter sa buhay nila.
Akala mo magtatagal ang relasyon. Akala mo matutupad ang pangarap. Akala mo magiging maayos ang lahat.
Pero may namatay.
At dahil doon, inisip mong tapos na rin ang kuwento mo.
Pero pinapatunayan ni Ruth: Minsan pinapayagan ng Diyos ang pagtatapos ng isang chapter dahil may covenant story Siyang inihahanda sa susunod.
Akala ni Naomi wala na siyang dala pagbalik niya. Pero hindi niya alam… dala niya si Ruth.
At si Ruth ay may dalang destiny.
Kalaunan nagkaanak sina Ruth at Boaz ng anak na si Obed. Si Obed naging ama ni Jesse. Si Jesse naging ama ni David.
At mula sa linyang iyon… dumating si Jesucristo.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hindi natin dapat husgahan agad ang kuwento habang nasa gitna pa tayo ng sakit.
Mukhang talunan ang Biyernes bago dumating ang Linggo ng pagkabuhay.
Mukhang katapusan ang krus bago dumating ang resurrection.
At baka ang sakit na pinagdadaanan mo ngayon ay hindi pa pala ang huling chapter.
Namatay sina Mahlon at Chilion bago tunay na nagsimula ang kuwento ni Ruth dahil minsan pinapayagan ng Diyos ang mga ending na hindi pa kayang maintindihan ng tao.
Pero ang Diyos ng Bibliya ay eksperto sa pagbuhay ng pag-asa mula sa mga guho.
Hindi nito binubura ang sakit. Tinutubos nito.
At baka dito nagiging personal ang lahat.
Dahil maraming taong tahimik na may libing sa puso.
Hindi lang pisikal na libing.
Libing ng dating sarili. Libing ng pangarap. Libing ng tiwala. Libing ng pag-asa.
At paulit-ulit mong tinatanong:
“Bakit ito namatay bago pa nagsimula ang kuwento ko?”
At marahang sumasagot si Ruth:
Dahil ang Diyos ay nagsusulat pa rin ng magagandang kuwento kahit pagkatapos ng mga libingan.
Kung may tinamaan dito sa puso mo, huwag kang mag-scroll na parang okay ka lang.
May mga taong isang hakbang na lang mula sa tuluyang pagsuko. Kailangan nilang marinig na hindi pa tapos ang Diyos magsulat ng redemption story.
May mga ending na hindi ibig sabihin iniwan ka ng Diyos. Minsan iyon ang pintuan kung saan tahimik nagsisimula ang redemption.
